title: Suffering and the Silence of God
subtitle: The problem of pain without the easy answers. Lament as the language faith speaks in the dark, the book of Job as God's refusal to explain, and how to hold on when heaven seems to have gone quiet.

connections.label: The Anxious Mind: Faith and Mental Health
Facing Death: The Last Enemy and the Sure Hope

parts.title: The Prayer That Hit the Ceiling
parts.body:
You prayed, and nothing happened. That is the part nobody warns you about. Not the suffering itself, though that is bad enough, the scan that came back wrong, the child who is not getting better, the marriage dissolving in slow motion, the grief that will not lift. The part nobody warns you about is the silence on the other end. You did what you were taught. You brought it to God, honestly, repeatedly, on your knees and in your car and at three in the morning, and the answer was a quiet so total that you began to wonder whether anyone had ever been listening at all.

And then a second wound opens underneath the first. You start doing the math you swore you would never do. If God is good, he would want to stop this. If God is all-powerful, he could stop this. He has not stopped this. The argument is old, older than Christianity, and it is sitting on your chest at two in the morning wearing the face of someone you love. The philosophers call it the problem of evil. You do not call it anything. You just feel the floor of your faith going soft.

Maybe the church handed you sentences that made it worse. God will not give you more than you can handle, which is not in the Bible, and which you know is a lie the first time you are handed more than you can handle. Everything happens for a reason, as if your suffering were a riddle God was withholding the answer to for sport. Just have faith, said by people who had never had their faith put through what yours was being put through. So you learned to say fine when asked, and to stop raising your hand in the prayer meeting, and to carry the question alone, because asking it out loud felt like a confession that you were losing your grip.

Let me say the thing I most want you to hear. The silence of God is not proof of the absence of God. It is one of the most common experiences in the whole of Scripture, and the Bible does not treat the people who cried into it as failures. It treats them as saints. The question that is breaking you is the question the Bible itself asks, out loud, more than a hundred times, and it never once tells the asker to be quiet. You are not at the edge of faith. You are at its oldest, most honest center.

parts.title: What the Silence Costs and What Is at Stake
parts.body:
It matters because the unanswered question does not stay quiet. It goes underground. Suffering that is never allowed to be spoken to God does not evaporate. It hardens into a low, polite distance, a faith you keep up out of habit while the trust has quietly died, a man who still attends and no longer expects anything, a woman who sings the words and means none of them. Pastors see this far more than the dramatic deconversion. The slow freeze is more common than the loud exit, and it is harder to thaw, because the person has not left. They are sitting in the third row, gone.

It matters because how the church handles suffering is the test it most often fails. We are good at celebration and clumsy at catastrophe. We know what to do with the wedding and not with the miscarriage, with the testimony of victory and not with the testimony that has no victory yet. And so the sufferer learns to suffer outside the building, which means the one place that should be a hospital becomes a stage, and the people in the most pain become the people who feel least welcome. I have done this. I have rushed past a grieving person with a verse because their grief frightened me, and I called my fear faithfulness.

It matters because the watching skeptic is standing right here, at exactly this question. The problem of evil is the single most common reason people give for walking away from God, and they are not wrong that it is a hard question. What they have usually never seen is a Christianity that does not flinch from it, that does not paper it over with a slogan, that can sit in the dark and grieve without letting go. When the church offers cheap answers, it confirms the skeptic's suspicion that faith is a refusal to look at reality. When the church can lament, something else becomes visible, a faith strong enough to hold the worst of the world in one hand and God in the other without pretending the worst is not real.

And it matters, finally, because you will not be the last to walk this road. Everyone you love will eventually stand where you are standing. Learning to suffer faithfully, and to sit with sufferers without fixing them, is not an advanced spiritual elective. It is the cost of loving anyone in a world where the wrong things still happen to the right people.

parts.title: What Scripture Actually Does With Pain
parts.body:
Start with the number, because it will surprise you. The largest single category of psalm in the Bible is the lament, the prayer of complaint, more of them than praise, more than thanksgiving, more than any other kind. The official songbook of the people of God is weighted toward sorrow addressed directly to God's face. How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever. Why do you hide your face from me. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. These are not the prayers of the faithless. These are the prayers Scripture canonized, kept, and taught its people to sing, which means God himself decided that the cry of the suffering belongs in the permanent worship of his church. You cannot be more honest with God than his own book trains you to be.

And then there is Psalm 88, which you should read when you are ready, because it is the one the church keeps for the bottom. It begins in darkness and it ends in darkness, and unlike almost every other lament it never turns the corner into hope. Its last word is darkness is my closest friend. The editors of Scripture put it there on purpose and left the lights off. There is a room in the house of faith with no resolution in it, kept for the nights you need it, and God built that room himself. He did not edit out the prayer that had no happy ending. He inspired it.

Then there is Job, and Job is the Bible's longest, most patient refusal to give you the answer you came for. A righteous man loses everything, his wealth, his children, his health, for reasons the reader is told and Job never is. His friends arrive and do what frightened religious people always do. They explain. You are suffering, so you must have sinned, because God is just and the just prosper. Every word they say is a true proverb misapplied like a hammer, and when God finally speaks from the whirlwind, he rebukes the friends, not Job. But notice what God does not do. He never tells Job why. He answers a hundred chapters of agonized questions with questions of his own, about the foundations of the earth and the wild goats and the storehouses of the snow, until Job is silenced, not by an explanation but by an encounter. The book of Job exists to tell you that the final answer to suffering is not a reason. It is a Presence. God does not hand Job a theodicy. He hands Job himself.

And this is where Christianity says the thing no other faith says. We do not have a God who explains suffering from a safe distance. We have a God who entered it. The cross is the place where the problem of evil stops being a debate and becomes a wound in God's own body. On the cross, the Son of God prays Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, which means the deepest cry of abandonment in the Bible is on the lips of God himself. He has been where you are. He has prayed the prayer that hit the ceiling. When Jesus stood at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, knowing he was about to raise him, knowing the ending was already in his hands, he wept anyway, because the right response of love to death is grief, even when you hold the cure. Christianity does not answer the problem of pain with a syllogism. It answers it with a God on a cross, and an empty tomb three days later, and the promise that the suffering, however long it runs, does not get the last word. Death is an enemy, Paul says, the last enemy to be destroyed. We do not make peace with it. We outlive it in Christ.

parts.title: The Church's Long Argument With Its Own Pain
parts.body:
The church has been wrestling with God over suffering for as long as there has been a church, and it has never settled the question, which is itself a kind of wisdom. The early Christians prayed the lament psalms as a matter of course, because they prayed the whole Psalter, and the Psalter does not skip the dark ones. Benedict's monks in the sixth century chanted all hundred and fifty psalms every week, the protests and the complaints alongside the praise, so that the dark prayers were always in the community's mouth, available to whoever needed them on any given week. The tradition assumed what we forgot, that the suffering are always in the room, and gave them a script written by God.

Augustine, writing his Confessions around the year 397, grieved openly, fought his own tears at his mother's funeral thinking a Christian should be above them, and then wept alone and offered the tears to God. He also wrote, across decades, some of the most serious reflection on evil the church has ever produced, refusing both the easy answer that evil is unreal and the despairing answer that God is not good. He landed on a hard and durable claim, that God would not permit evil at all unless he were powerful and good enough to bring good out of it, a claim that explains nothing about your particular sorrow and yet has held millions steady through theirs.

The middle of the fourteenth century brought the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third of Europe, and the church did not respond with tidy theodicy. It responded with the plague saints, the burial of the dead at terrible risk, and a deepened literature of lament. Out of the same century came Julian of Norwich, who nearly died, received her visions of the suffering Christ, and wrote the line the church has clung to ever since, that all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Read in context it is not a denial of pain. She had stared straight at the cross. It is a defiant trust spoken from inside the dark, which is the only place trust like that can be spoken.

The Reformers knew the silence too. Luther had a word for the seasons when God seemed not merely silent but hostile, Anfechtung, the assault, and he refused to be ashamed of them, counseling sufferers to eat, to seek company, to speak the promises out loud against their own minds. And in the centuries since, the church's best witnesses on suffering have almost always been people who suffered. Charles Spurgeon preached through crushing depression. Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote his deepest prayers from a Nazi prison cell, and was hanged at Flossenbürg in April 1945, weeks before the war ended, having written that only a suffering God can help. Corrie ten Boom watched her sister die in Ravensbrück and came out preaching forgiveness. None of them solved the problem of evil. All of them held onto God inside it, and that holding on, passed from hand to hand across twenty centuries, is the church's real answer, not a proof but a people who would not let go.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Suffering has been studied from every angle outside the church, by philosophers, psychologists, and physicians, and the believer has nothing to fear from any of it. All truth is God's truth, and honest work on pain often confirms what Scripture assumed. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each gets right, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of suffering carries a hidden picture of what a human being is and what they are for, and the picture is where the argument lives.

secular.author: Viktor Frankl
secular.whatItGetsRight: Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived Auschwitz, observed that those who endured the camps were not the strongest or the cleverest but the ones who held onto a why, a meaning that the suffering could not erase. He built a whole therapy on it, the conviction that a person can bear almost any how if they have a why, and that meaning is not given by circumstances but chosen in the teeth of them. Few books have witnessed more clearly that the human spirit needs more than comfort to survive.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Frankl saw that meaning sustains, and Scripture agrees, but it asks where the meaning comes from. Frankl locates the why inside the sufferer, a meaning each person must manufacture, which works until the day the manufacturing fails. Scripture locates the why outside the sufferer, in a God who suffered, in a resurrection that is promised rather than invented. The difference is whether your meaning is a flame you must keep lit by willpower or a fire that was burning before you and will burn after you. Frankl gives the dying man a reason to stand. The gospel gives him a reason that does not depend on his standing.

secular.source: The Problem of Pain and A Grief Observed
secular.author: C. S. Lewis
secular.whatItGetsRight: Lewis wrote the careful philosophical defense first, arguing that pain is God's megaphone to rouse a deaf world and that a world of free creatures must be a world where they can wound each other. Then his wife died, and he wrote the second book, raw and furious, recording how the tidy arguments felt like sandcastles before the wave of actual grief. The two books together are honest in a way one alone could never be, a man who built the theory and then watched it tested in his own ruin, and refused to pretend the test was easy.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Lewis at his best is doing exactly what Scripture does, holding the argument and the agony together without letting either silence the other. Where even Lewis can drift is toward making pain primarily instructive, a lesson God is teaching, which Scripture allows but does not require. Job is never told his suffering was a lesson, and the cross is not God teaching us something so much as God bearing something. Lewis is most biblical not in the megaphone theory but in A Grief Observed, where he stops explaining and starts crying out, which is precisely what the Psalms do. The theory is useful. The lament is truer.

secular.source: The Varieties of Religious Experience and the study of the dark night
secular.author: William James and the psychology of religion
secular.whatItGetsRight: James and the field after him documented that profound spiritual experience routinely passes through darkness, that the felt absence of God is a near-universal feature of serious religious life rather than a malfunction of it. The psychology of religion has confirmed that doubt, dryness, and the sense of divine silence are normal stages, not signs of a faith failing. This is a real correction to the modern assumption that genuine spirituality should feel warm and certain.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture knew the dark night long before psychology named it, and the mystics who described it, John of the Cross above all, were charting territory the Psalms already mapped. Where the psychological account stops is at the question of whether anyone is actually there in the dark. James can tell you the experience of silence is common and even fruitful. He cannot tell you whether the silence is empty or whether it is the hiddenness of a God who is present and not yet speaking. Scripture insists it is the latter, that the God who feels absent in Psalm 88 is the same God who raised Jesus, and that the dark is real but not final.

secular.source: The contemporary problem of evil debate
secular.author: Modern analytic philosophy of religion
secular.whatItGetsRight: Philosophers have sharpened the problem of evil into its strongest forms and have done the church a service by refusing easy answers. The honest atheist who says a good and powerful God would not permit a child to suffer is naming a real difficulty, and the believing philosophers who have answered, Alvin Plantinga among them, have shown with rigor that the bare logical contradiction does not hold, that the existence of God and the existence of evil are not strictly incompatible. The argument has been clarified on both sides.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The philosophy can show that God and evil are not a logical contradiction, which is worth knowing, and it cannot do the thing the sufferer actually needs. Scripture never answers Job with a proof. It answers him with a Presence, and then it answers the whole problem with a cross. The believer can be grateful that the logical defense holds while recognizing that no one was ever consoled by a syllogism at a graveside. The intellectual problem and the personal anguish are different problems, and Scripture meets the second one not with an argument but with a God who entered the suffering himself. The philosophy clears the ground. Only the gospel fills it.

secular.source: Trauma research and the body's memory of suffering
secular.author: Bessel van der Kolk and the trauma field
secular.whatItGetsRight: The trauma research established that overwhelming suffering is stored in the body, not only the memory, that a nervous system can stay locked on alarm years after the danger has passed, and that recovery has to involve the body and not only the mind. For Christians taught to treat suffering as a purely spiritual matter, this is a needed correction. The sufferer is not weak for being unable to think their way out of what their body is still carrying.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture agrees the body keeps score. David says his bones wasted away while he kept silent, and the lament psalms are full of physical anguish, withered strength, sleepless eyes, a heart like wax. But the trauma frame contains injury and recovery with no sin to confess and no resurrection to hope for, which is true as far as it goes and stops short of the whole person. A sufferer is more than a damaged nervous system to be regulated. They are a creature with a future that medicine cannot reach, whose final healing is not a calmer baseline but a raised body. The science is a real gift for the road. It is not a destination.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Bible and stand at the same gravesides still account for suffering along two different lines, and the difference is ancient and serious. It runs to how much of suffering we should attribute to the direct ordaining hand of God and how much to the disorder of a fallen world he permits but does not author. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to protect something true about God, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: God ordains all things, and suffering is held inside his sovereign purpose
views.body: This view begins with the conviction that nothing falls outside the rule of God, that not a sparrow drops without the Father, and that to remove suffering from his sovereign hand is to leave the sufferer in a universe that is finally out of control. The God of this view is not standing back helplessly while evil runs loose. He reigns over it, bends it, and will bring from it a good that the sufferer cannot yet see, as he did supremely at the cross, where the worst evil ever committed became the means of the world's salvation. Joseph said to the brothers who sold him, you meant it for evil, but God meant it for good, and this view takes that sentence as the pattern of all suffering. Advocates insist this is not coldness but the deepest comfort, because a pain that God has purposed is a pain that means something, and the alternative, a suffering that is simply loose in the world, is far more terrifying. They are guarding against a real danger, a small and reactive God who is as surprised by your tragedy as you are, who cannot promise that any of it will be redeemed because he did not see it coming. Against that, they hold the high view, that the hand on your life in the dark is the same hand that holds the stars, and that nothing it permits is wasted. And they are careful, the wisest of them, never to say this to the freshly bereaved as an explanation, because Job's friends had the doctrine right and the timing monstrous.

views.view: God permits suffering in a broken world and stands against it as enemy, not author
views.body: This view begins with the conviction that God is not the author of evil, that he calls it an enemy and means to destroy it, and that much suffering is the wreckage of a creation in rebellion rather than the direct script of heaven. The God of this view did not send the cancer or will the abuse. He hates them, weeps over them as Jesus wept at the tomb, and works to redeem them without having authored them. When a tower fell and killed eighteen, Jesus refused to read it as a verdict on the victims, which this view takes as a warning against assigning every tragedy a divine intention. Advocates insist this is not a weak God but a holy one, a God too good to be the maker of the very evil he died to defeat, and they find deep comfort in a heaven that is on their side against the suffering rather than behind it. They are guarding against a real danger too, a picture of God in which he becomes the secret cause of every horror, the author of the abuse and the architect of the disease, a picture that has driven many sufferers to hate the God they were told to thank. Against that, they hold that God is light and in him is no darkness at all, that he is found not behind the evil but inside it with you, suffering it alongside you, and committed to its final undoing. And they are careful, the wisest of them, never to use this to imply God is helpless, because a God who cannot finally defeat what he hates is no comfort at all.

parts.title: What God Forms in the Dark
parts.body:
I have to say this part carefully, because it can curdle into the cruelty that tells a suffering person their pain is a divine teaching tool, as if God broke their life to improve their character. I am not saying that. I am saying something narrower and, I think, truer. The God who meets people in the dark has a habit of forming things there that the daylight never produces, and naming them is not the same as justifying the dark. The dark remains an enemy. And God works in it anyway.

He forms a faith that no longer depends on circumstances. The believer who has only ever known God in the good seasons has a faith that has never been weighed, and they do not know what it can hold until it is asked to hold everything. The one who keeps praying into the silence, who shows up to a God who seems to have gone quiet and refuses to leave, is being forged into something the comfortable never become. Job said, though he slay me, yet will I trust him, and that sentence cannot be spoken from a comfortable chair. It is only available on the ash heap. The faith that survives the silence is the only faith that was ever worth having, because it is no longer attached to the gifts. It is attached to the Giver.

He forms compassion that has teeth. Ask in any congregation who the people are that sit longest with the suffering, who answer the phone at three in the morning and do not flinch and do not reach for a verse like a citation, and they will almost always be people who have suffered. Paul says God comforts us in our affliction so that we can comfort others with the comfort we ourselves received. The comfort is meant to travel. The one who has been met in the dark becomes the church's best company for the next person in it, because they have lost the urge to explain and learned the harder art of simply staying.

And he forms a strange and durable hope, the kind that is not optimism. Optimism believes things will get better. This hope believes that even if they do not, the story does not end here, that the God who raised Jesus from a real grave will raise you too, and that the silence is not the absence of God but the hiddenness of a God who has not finished speaking. The last pages of the Bible do not promise a world where suffering never happened. They promise a God who will wipe away every tear from their eyes, which means the tears were real all the way to the end, and the hands that finally dry them are his. The believer formed in the dark carries that hope not as a feeling but as a fact they are holding onto with both hands, and on the worst nights, holding on is enough. Holding on is faith.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: None of this is meant to be admired from a distance. It is meant to be done, slowly, and mostly it is the work of staying when leaving would be easier. Two things before the list. First, if you are suffering, you do not have to suffer alone, and the instinct to hide your pain from God and from people is the very thing that will deepen it. Tell someone the truth this week. Second, and read this twice. If the suffering has brought you to the edge, if you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the United States, right now, and tell someone who loves you. Do not wait for morning. Your life is not a problem to be solved. It is a gift God is not finished giving, even on the night you cannot feel it.

steps: Pray one lament psalm out loud each day, and pray it as your own. Start with Psalm 13, then 42, then 88. Do not soften the words. Let the Bible say to God what you have been afraid to say.

Tell one safe person the actual truth about where your faith is, not the polished version. Say the sentence you have been rehearsing alone, the one about the silence, the one about the doubt. Saying it out loud is not unbelief. It is honesty, and God can work with honesty.

Stop trying to feel something when you pray. Show up to the silence and stay in it for ten minutes, and let your presence be the prayer when the words are gone. You are not performing for God. You are sitting with him.

Refuse the cheap answers, including the ones in your own head. When the voice says you must have done something to deserve this, or that real faith would have fixed it by now, answer it with Job, whom God called right and his friends wrong.

Read the book of Job slowly, a few chapters at a time, and watch what God does and does not do at the end. Let it free you from the demand for an explanation, and from the friends who keep trying to supply one.

If the suffering has frozen you, if you cannot function, if you are sinking, call a counselor, a doctor, or a pastor. God heals through means, through skilled people, the way he feeds through farmers, and asking for help is faith walking toward the help God provides.

Find one person who has walked through something like what you are walking through, and ask them how they held on. The church's real answer to suffering is passed hand to hand, not handed down from a podium.

Build a floor under your week, the things that keep a suffering body alive, sleep at a regular hour, food, a walk outside, a little daylight. The lament psalms are full of bodies. Tend yours. It is part of the prayer.

Stay in a worshiping community even when you feel nothing, and let them carry the faith you cannot currently hold. There are seasons when the right thing is to be carried, and the body of Christ exists for exactly those seasons.

Memorize one passage of presence until it is available at three in the morning, Psalm 23, or Romans 8 from verse 35 to the end, or Isaiah 43 from verse 1. Not as a charm against the dark. As furniture for it.

Practice the slow art of staying with other sufferers, sitting without fixing, saying little, the way Job's friends did right for seven days before they ruined it by speaking. The comfort you have received is meant to travel.

Hold the question and God at the same time. You do not have to resolve the problem of evil to keep believing. You only have to keep coming, hands open, refusing to let go of him with one hand while you shake the other at the sky. That two-handed grip is what the Bible calls faith.

Let your suffering, when it has aged into something you can carry, become a door for someone else. The people the church most needs in its hardest rooms are the ones who have been in those rooms and did not let go of God.

Build a theology of suffering before you need it, by reading the church's witnesses who suffered, Bonhoeffer, Spurgeon, Julian of Norwich, ten Boom, so that when the next dark comes, you are not building the house in the storm.

Keep returning to the cross, where the problem of evil became a wound in God's own body, and to the empty tomb, where it was answered not with a reason but with a resurrection. This is the long meditation that holds a life steady, that God did not explain your suffering from a distance. He entered it.

Number your days, and let the reality of your own mortality teach you what to stop wasting your life on and what to receive as gift. The wise are not the ones who escaped suffering. They are the ones who let it make them awake, awake to God, and awake to the morning he has promised is coming.
